Then the prospect leaned in and said, "nobody here can tell me what changed." Nobody else on their side could say what we had changed in the first six months.

That hit me: the value was real and it lived in one person's head. When that person left, the story vanished.

Since then I make sure to write the before‑and‑after down while the champion is still there to confirm it. It’s the only way to keep the value alive when the team changes.

- In my case, I wanted to know what software they run.

body:
A sales leader told me they were dreading one question: "why are we paying $40K a year for ZoomInfo".

I built a TAM of Australian dental off public data. The paid spend I can trace comes to roughly $30 to $35, plus a flat subscription for the decision-maker lookups.

It also took seven weeks.

What came out: about 10,500 businesses, 14,000 locations, 25,000 named clinicians and 5,600 decision makers.

The word that matters there is named. Every clinician is a name on the practice's own team page or booking roster, checked against the page in code. A headcount field can't tell you how many dentists work at a two-chair practice.

The association register listed one big chain at 6 locations. Its own website lists 171.

A model saying "12 dentists" was wrong far more often than a list of names checked against the page. So the models read and the code checks every name. Two cheap ones read 6,818 practice websites for $16.40, and the same job run as Claude agents worked out at about $3,397.

The seven weeks went on five drafts. It's cheap in money and expensive in hours, and ZoomInfo is the reverse.

For anyone leading an outbound team that sells into one industry, here's my system:

- Start from the regulator's or licensing body's count, so you know roughly what complete looks like.
- Stack every free list the industry has: map data, the association register, booking or scheduling platforms with public pages, government registers.
- Read each source's terms before pulling from it.
- Count chains from their own websites.
- Size every business by the named people on its own pages, booking rosters included.
- Check a small sample by hand before counting anything, then score yourself against it.
- Mark an unreadable page as unread, never as zero.
- Use the Wayback Machine for sites that no longer load.

What does the licensing body count in your market, and how close does your TAM get to it?

"This is the most comprehensive TAM we've ever had."

A client's salesperson said that about a TAM I built of 10,500 Australian dental businesses, all from public data.

It runs on my Claude Max plan and a Blitz subscription, plus roughly $7 to $25 a build in everything else.

The usual TAM is a ZoomInfo or Apollo export filtered by industry and employee count, and the reps find out on the phone which accounts were worth the call.

That client sizes accounts by clinicians, and six or more is where it's worth their while. So the build counted them by name, and came out at:
- 14,000 locations
- 25,000 clinicians, each a named person on the practice's own site or booking page
- 5,600 decision makers
- about 1,350 accounts with six or more clinicians, flagged before anyone dialled

To build your own, I'd use Claude Code. Codex would work too.

Decide what makes an account worth calling
- Clinicians, for that client
- Yours might be seats or sites. Anything a business publishes about itself can be a column

Find out what complete looks like
- A regulator, a licensing body, the trade association or a government count

Pull every public list the market appears on
- Maps and directories
- Any software the industry books or buys through. In dental, a booking platform listed every practitioner
- Check each source's terms first

Let AI read every website
- Two cheap models read 6,818 practice websites for $16.40
- Check every name the models return against the page it came from

Check it before a rep touches it
- Before counting anything, check a small sample by hand and score the whole build against it
- The register had one dental chain at 6 sites. Its own website lists 171

The first dental draft took about a week. It's a skill now: GP, physio, psychology, speech, OT, orthopaedics and chiro since, and every build after GP took under a week.

If you want to see what this would look like for your market, send me a DM.

43,789 board papers, read across 1,541 public boards.

106 organisations qualified on the first pass. 52 held up.

Board papers are a board and its senior executives talking about their priorities, in a public forum and on the record. There's no stronger signal.

And what gets agreed is often checked at the next board meeting, so whatever they committed to has to be followed up in the meetings after it.

Across 2,390 US boards, the papers came from school districts, utilities and transit, universities, pension systems, counties, cities and public hospitals. We only looked at the US. It might hold globally, because a lot of public institutions release their board minutes.

They sit on each board's own website and archive pages, in links inside agenda PDFs, in council meeting systems and in meeting video captions. Inside are current-year audit plans, audit findings and risk reports, all dated.

If you sell into public bodies, the work is getting through the noise to the signal.

We were hunting one specific risk named in an audit plan. The noise:

- 28 were "vendor management" that meant towing contracts, golf concessions and ambulance response times
- 9 were the wrong government. Three Springfields, two Orange Counties

Volume is noise too. One county had posted 21,184 papers, so we capped each government at 150.

That search finished at 63 accounts.

Some noise looks like silence. Once, 604 boards came back "nothing found" because the reader had failed, and 338 of 368 batches were never read.

More and more outbound teams write their messaging with AI.

I've been guilty of it. And I often end up rewriting more than it would have taken to write the message myself.

Meanwhile the thing AI is good at sits underused: looking at vast amounts of data, pulling different sources together, bringing different tools together.

That's the targeting half of outbound. Working out who is worth a message at all.

The writing half, I think humans are still best at. We outsourced that as well.

If you lead an outbound team, that's the split worth checking.

The order I'd do it in:

- AI does the data work.
- Someone on the team writes the first attempt at the message. Even if it's only the structure.
- Then AI improves it and applies it across accounts.

Which half has your team handed over?

For one client, I had AI write outbound sequences.

Some went through multiple rounds of rewriting, and it was bad. Others came out much closer to right.

The rewriting was on the platform-level messaging, general in nature. The ones that came out closer sat on hyper-specific targeting.

I think a lot of that was the targeting.

When the targeting is loose, AI struggles. It makes stuff up, and there's no consistency from one message to the next.

Make it hyper-specific and the AI writes to that specificity. The messaging is often better.

If you lead an outbound team, check which sequences your reps rewrite most.

I'd still outsource the data work to AI. It's good at looking at vast amounts of data and pulling different sources together.

For the message, give it some structure first. Your own first attempt at how you'd lay it out.

Then get it to improve that, and apply it across accounts.

body:
After six years in New York, our first kid was born and we moved home to Australia.

I hadn't worked out what came next.

Going out on my own had been in the back of my mind for a while. Moving home forced it.

I did it straight away. I also got to be home for a long stretch after she was born, and I felt lucky to have that.

Back at the consulting firm, I was at the whims of my employer and of my clients. Meetings got booked at the last minute. I didn't pick the clients or the time zones. The one I still remember is being on holiday and having to join a meeting, because that's when the client needed it.

Now the hard stop is a kindergarten.

Our kid goes to a community kindy that shuts at four o'clock. You have to be there by four. My wife and I juggle pickup, and when she can't, I do. The laptop closes around 4.30, stays closed until the kids are in bed, then opens again so I can finish a few things.

It costs me. I say no to meetings. I probably can't take on an extra client. That's a trade I'm willing to make right now.

Recently I told a client I couldn't make some of their meetings because of pickup. I'm not hiding it. I'm picking clients as much as they're picking me, and that works when our values line up. I'm not taking the piss with it, either.

It changed how I work for myself too. I built my own tracker for effective hourly rate and utilisation. The goal is about 40 hours a week, at 70 to 85 per cent utilisation. Then it's trade-offs, and I push as much as I can through Claude Code to speed things up and automate where it makes sense.

The kindy still shuts at four.

The 8 ways I detect what software a company runs
(3 of which hardly anyone in go-to-market uses).

Website code
→ Most tools leave a script or tag in the site's code.
→ I download the website locally, then scan the HTML for different things.
→ The software often turns up as a byproduct of that scanning.
→ One build found 915 booking systems across 1,933 sites.
→ Pro: cheap, and the best fit for customer-facing tools.
→ Con: it only sees the website. Back-office tools stay invisible.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: everywhere.

Job ads
→ Ads list the tools candidates need to know.
→ Pro: it picks up back-office tools that never touch the website.
→ Con: it's inferred. The ad might be old, or name the tool they're leaving.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: everywhere.

The vendor's own proof
→ Customer logos and case studies on the vendor's site.
→ Pro: rarely wrong. A few vendors publish a finder that lists every customer.
→ Con: usually small numbers, and only the happy customers.
→ Effort to use: easy.
→ Used in GTM: often.

Their integration and privacy pages
→ Companies name the tools they plug into.
→ Privacy policies often list the suppliers that touch customer data.
→ Pro: the best evidence there is, because they wrote it.
→ Con: most never say, and it means reading a lot of pages.
→ Effort to use: medium.
→ Used in GTM: sometimes.

DNS records
→ Every domain publishes where its email goes and which apps it verified.
→ Pro: someone had to set each record up, so it's hard to fake.
→ Strongest on email and security tools.
→ Con: no proof of live use. Old records outlive the tool.
→ Effort to use: hard.
→ Used in GTM: rarely.

Network banners
→ Scanners check every server online and log what software answers.
→ Pro: it finds the firewall or VPN nothing else can see.
→ Con: hard to tie a server to a company. No proof of live use.
→ Effort to use: hard.
→ Used in GTM: barely.

Login portals
→ Some tools give each customer their own address, like acme.vendor.com.
→ Pro: close to a yes or no. The portal exists or it doesn't.
→ Con: only works for tools built that way.
→ Some answer for any name you make up, so test a fake one first.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it.
→ Used in GTM: barely.

Password reset checks
→ Put a work email into a tool's "forgot password" page.
→ Plenty of tools answer differently when the account exists.
→ Pro: it confirms a named person has an account.
→ Con: one email at a time, and that person may get a reset email.
→ Effort to use: hard, you build it.
→ Used in GTM: barely.

Which one I reach for depends on how the software shows up.
Usually it's a few.

When a tool shows up through two of these, I trust it more.

Which ones have I missed?

One SDR for every 4.7 net-new sellers.

That's about where US software companies sit, in each size band from 51 to 1,000 employees. Past 1,000, the number stops holding.

It started with a dataset of 21,783 US sales teams where the role counts looked wrong. Managers outnumbered reps at a lot of companies and SDRs looked undercounted.

In a 20-company test, the 2,700 people the file called managers were mostly account managers and directors. Front-line sales managers came to 443.

Rather than throw the SDR question away, I recounted it from LinkedIn. 2,206 US software companies. 12,314 SDRs against 89,697 net-new sellers. Anyone working existing customers is left out, account managers included.

Net-new sellers per SDR:

51 to 200 employees: 4.8
201 to 500: 4.7
501 to 1,000: 4.6
1,001 to 5,000: 6.2
5,001 to 10,000: 10.0
10,000+: 14.2

If you're building an SDR team somewhere under 1,000 people, that's the ratio your peers have.

Above 1,000 employees, SDR coverage falls to a third.

Taking out each band's 10 biggest teams doesn't change the shape. Even counting every inside sales rep at the 5,000+ companies as an SDR, that band only gets to 7.7.

The original file said 47% of these companies had an SDR. The recount says 70%.

What I can't tell you is why it drops. I only counted US profiles, so an SDR team based overseas doesn't show up, and that might be part of it. More inbound demand could be another. So could AEs prospecting their own named accounts. I haven't checked any of them.

If you've taken an SDR team past 1,000 employees, what changed first?

A cold email told me about my two person team.

There's one of me. That's the easy mistake to spot.

It opened on my own work: "Your work mapping OSHA citations and accreditation issues into prospect lists is a smart take on pain based targeting."

Nothing in that line is news to me. It's my own work, played back to me, probably off my LinkedIn.

Then it starts guessing.

The OSHA citations are for my clients. Slingshot GTM is a consultancy, and I'm not mapping citations for my own prospecting. So the pitch, "more inbound pull behind those pain signals so your outreach lands warmer", is aimed at lists I build for other people.

It assumes I'm not doing inbound. I might be. They don't know.

And the offer is a brand story. I don't care about the brand story.

If your SDRs write cold email, compare it with what they could have sent:

"slingshotgtm.com has three pages: the homepage, a booking page and one case study. Nothing for Slingshot GTM in the LinkedIn, Google or Meta ad libraries.

So it looks like your clients come from your posts and referrals. That might be exactly how you want it.

If it is, ignore this. If it isn't, is inbound something you've ruled out, or something nobody's built yet?"

They could have checked all of that from the outside. And it asks the inbound question the first email guessed at.

The first email ended by offering to write me a few short ideas.

Writing them would have been the email.

body:
This is why cold email is broken:

What I received:

I'd bet an AI wrote it off the back of my LinkedIn. It played my own work back to me and didn't understand the context.

- "A two person team." There's one of me.
- The OSHA citations are for my clients. Slingshot GTM is a consultancy, and I'm not mapping citations for my own prospecting. So "more inbound pull behind those pain signals so your outreach lands warmer" is aimed at lists I build for other people.
- It assumes I'm not doing inbound. I might be.
- The offer is a brand story. I don't care about the brand story.

What they should've sent:

"slingshotgtm.com has three pages: the homepage, a booking page and one case study. Nothing for Slingshot GTM in the LinkedIn, Google or Meta ad libraries.

So it looks like your clients come from your posts and referrals. That might be exactly how you want it.

If it is, ignore this. If it isn't, is inbound something you've ruled out, or something nobody's built yet?"

They could have checked all of it from the outside. And it asks the inbound question the first email answered for me.

The first email offered to write me a few short ideas.

Writing them would have been the email.
